title: Redesigning a kitting cart to cut changeover time on a CNC cell
summary: The cart is the changeover. Reorganize what rides on it and the spindle stops waiting on the walk.

blocks.title: The changeover happens at the cart, not the machine
blocks.body: Time a CNC cell changeover and most of the minutes are not cutting or even touching the machine - they are walking, hunting, and returning for the thing that should have been within reach. A kitting cart redesigned around the actual job sequence closes that gap. Example numbers below from a fictional two-machine cell running a family of four parts.

blocks.heading: Where the minutes go today
blocks.body: Observed changeover on the example cell: 47 minutes spindle-to-spindle. Of that, 11 minutes were walking to the tool crib and back (six trips), 7 minutes hunting for the right soft jaws and the correct offset sheet, and 4 minutes returning a dropped collet and re-finding the torque wrench. Only 25 minutes were work that must happen at the machine. The cart as it exists is a flat rolling table - everything rides in one pile, oldest jobs' leftovers included.

blocks.heading: Before and after the redesign (example numbers)
rows: Job kit pre-staged on the cart before the last part finishes
Shadow-board layout: every item has one labeled home
Tools preset in holders, arranged in setup order
Offset sheet laminated on the cart top, no transcription errors
blocks.caption: One fictional cell, four-part family, second shift. Your numbers will differ; the shape usually does not.

blocks.heading: The redesigned cart in three zones

nodes.title: Zone 1 - This job
nodes.detail: Top shelf. Only the active job: preset tools in setup order, soft jaws, gages, laminated offset sheet. Nothing else is allowed here.

nodes.title: Zone 2 - Next job
nodes.detail: Middle shelf. The kit for the next part number, staged while the spindle is still cutting. Changeover starts already half done.

nodes.title: Zone 3 - Returns
nodes.detail: Bottom shelf. Everything coming off the machine lands here, unsorted. Sorting happens at the crib, not beside the machine.

items.label: One job per zone, no overflow
items.detail: If Zone 1 has leftovers from the last job, the system is already broken.

items.label: The kit is built during cycle time
items.detail: Kitting is internal work moved external - the core of the whole changeover cut.

items.label: Shadow-board everything
items.detail: A missing item must be visible from three feet away, before the machine stops.

items.label: The cart goes home at shift end
items.detail: Returns emptied, kits for tomorrow's first two jobs staged.

columns.name: Buy a commercial cart
columns.detail: Fast, $800-2,500, and never quite fits your tooling. Good when the cell runs catalog toolholders and standard jaws.

columns.name: Build in-house
columns.detail: A week of shop time, fits the exact job family, and the team that builds it believes in it. Good when setups repeat weekly and the tooling is idiosyncratic.

columns.name: Modify what you have
columns.detail: Add shelves and a shadow board to the existing table for under $100. The right first move almost everywhere - prove the zones before buying steel.

blocks.title: The failure mode
blocks.body: A kitting cart fails socially before it fails mechanically. If the crib keeps pulling tools off the staged cart for emergencies, Zone 2 is empty by changeover and the whole design is dead in a month. The cart's inventory has to be treated as committed, like material already issued to a job.
